title: Frame of Reference, Relative Motion & The Vector Divide: Distance vs Displacement Mechanics
description: Master the relativity of motion, reference points (origin), and the foundational distinction between scalar distance and vector displacement in 1D kinematics.
subtopics: Reference Points & Origin: Why motion is relative to the observer's frame
Motion in a Straight Line: 1D coordinate axis with positive and negative directions
Distance: Total path length traversed by an object (scalar, always positive)
Displacement: Shortest straight-line vector distance from initial to final position (vector, can be zero or negative)
Displacement vs Distance Invariant: Magnitude of displacement is always <= total distance
Zero Displacement Paradox: Closed loops, circular tracks, and round trips
key_concepts: Relativity of Motion: An object may be perceived as moving by one observer and stationary by another depending on the reference frame.
Reference Point (Origin): The fixed landmark or coordinate origin from which all spatial positions are measured.
Distance (Scalar): Total ground path covered by a body, possessing magnitude only and never decreasing with time.
Displacement (Vector): Shortest directed straight-line segment from initial position to final position, possessing both magnitude and direction.
Geometric Bound: Displacement magnitude is always less than or equal to distance traveled (|s| <= d); equality holds only for straight line motion without reversing.
Zero Displacement Scenario: When an object returns to its starting point, displacement is exactly zero even if thousands of meters were traveled.
success_criteria: Student can specify reference frames, calculate distance vs displacement for linear and circular paths, and prove why displacement can be zero while distance is non-zero.
chapter_notes:
### 4.1 Reference Points and the Relativity of Motion
Motion is a change in the position of an object over time **relative to a reference frame**.
- A passenger seated in a moving train appears stationary to a fellow passenger (same reference frame), but appears moving at high speed to an observer on the platform.
- To specify position, we establish a **reference point** called the **Origin ($O$)**.

### 4.2 Distance vs Displacement
| Diagnostic Property | Distance ($d$) | Displacement ($ec{s}$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Physical Nature** | **Scalar quantity** (Magnitude only) | **Vector quantity** (Magnitude + Direction) |
| **Definition** | Actual length of the entire path traversed | Shortest straight-line distance from Initial ($A$) to Final ($B$) point |
| **Sign & Value** | Always positive ($d > 0$) for moving body; cannot decrease | Can be **positive, zero, or negative** depending on direction |
| **Zero Value** | Cannot be zero if object has moved | **Can be zero** if initial and final positions coincide |
| **Fundamental Invariant** | $d \ge |ec{s}|$ | $|ec{s}| \le d$ (Equal only in straight line motion in one direction) |

### 4.3 Classic Examination Scenarios
1. **Circular Track**: An athlete runs around a circular track of radius $r$.
   - For 1 full round: Distance $= 2\pi r$, Displacement $= 0$.
   - For half round: Distance $= \pi r$, Displacement $= 2r$ (diameter).
2. **Farmer along Square Field**: A farmer moves along boundary of square field of side $10\text{ m}$ in $40\text{ s}$.
   - Side $= 10\text{ m}$, Perimeter $= 40\text{ m}$. Speed $= 1\text{ m/s}$.
   - In $2\text{ min } 20\text{ s} = 140\text{ s}$: Rounds $= 140/40 = 3.5$.
   - Final position is diagonally opposite: Displacement $= \sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.14\text{ m}$.

worked_examples.problem: A passenger sitting in a moving train observes the trees outside moving backward while fellow passengers appear stationary. Explain this using the concept of reference frames.
worked_examples.given: Train moving forward with velocity $v$. Observers: passenger inside train vs observer standing on ground platform.
worked_examples.substitution: With respect to the passenger (train frame), fellow passengers have zero relative velocity; stationary roadside trees move backward at $-\vec{v}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Motion is not absolute; it is defined only relative to a chosen reference frame.
2. In the train's frame of reference, coordinates of seated passengers do not change ($\Delta x = 0$).
3. Stationary trees on the ground are moving backward with velocity $-v$ relative to the moving train frame.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Motion is relative to the chosen reference frame: fellow passengers share the same frame (stationary), whereas trees outside have a backward relative velocity.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.1: Reference frame of moving train relative to platform

worked_examples.problem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 200 m in 40 s. What will be the distance covered and the displacement at the end of 2 minutes 20 seconds?
worked_examples.given: Diameter $D = 200\text{ m} \implies r = 100\text{ m}$. Time for 1 round $T = 40\text{ s}$. Total time $t = 2\text{ min } 20\text{ s} = 140\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.formula: Number of rounds $n = \frac{t}{T}$; Distance $s = n \times 2\pi r$; Displacement = Straight-line distance between initial and final position.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. In $3.5$ rounds, the athlete completes 3 full laps and ends up diametrically opposite to the start point.
2. Total Distance $= 3.5 \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 100 = 3.5 \times 628.57 = \mathbf{2200\text{ m}}$.
3. Initial and final points are opposite ends of the diameter. Net Displacement $= 2r = D = \mathbf{200\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Distance covered = 2200 m; Magnitude of displacement = 200 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.3: Circular track motion with diametrical displacement vector

worked_examples.problem: A farmer moves along the boundary of a square field of side 10 m in 40 s. What will be the magnitude of displacement of the farmer at the end of 2 minutes 20 seconds from his initial position?
worked_examples.given: Square side $L = 10\text{ m}$. Perimeter $P = 4 \times 10 = 40\text{ m}$. Time for 1 round $= 40\text{ s}$. Total time $t = 140\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.formula: Rounds $n = \frac{140}{40} = 3.5$. Displacement across diagonal $= \sqrt{L^2 + L^2} = L\sqrt{2}$.
worked_examples.substitution: After 3.5 rounds, the farmer is at the opposite diagonal corner: $\text{Displacement} = 10\sqrt{2}\text{ m}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Distance in 140 s $= \frac{40\text{ m}}{40\text{ s}} \times 140\text{ s} = 140\text{ m}$ (3.5 laps).
2. Farmer starts at corner A, completes 3 full laps back at A, then travels another 2 sides (AB + BC = 20 m) ending at corner C.
3. Straight-line displacement $|AC| = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{14.14\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Magnitude of displacement = 14.14 m (along the diagonal).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.4: Square field trajectory and Pythagorean diagonal displacement

worked_examples.problem: Can the magnitude of displacement ever be greater than the distance traveled by an object? State the precise condition under which distance equals displacement.
worked_examples.given: Arbitrary curvilinear vs rectilinear 1D path.
worked_examples.substitution: Displacement is the shortest straight-line chord; distance is the integrated arc length along the trajectory.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. The shortest distance between two points in Euclidean space is a straight line.
2. Any deviation, curvature, or reversal of direction increases path length ($d$) without increasing displacement ($|\vec{s}|$).
3. Therefore, $|\vec{s}| \le d$ holds universally.
4. Equality ($|\vec{s}| = d$) holds if and only if the object moves in a straight line in a constant, unchanging direction.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: No, displacement can never exceed distance ($|\vec{s}| \le d$); they are equal only during unidirectional straight-line motion.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.2: Distance (curved path) vs Displacement (straight line vector)

worked_examples.problem: An object moves 3 m North, then 4 m East. Calculate: (a) Total distance traveled, and (b) Net displacement vector and direction.
worked_examples.given: Displacement 1: $\vec{s}_1 = 3\hat{j}\text{ m}$ (North); Displacement 2: $\vec{s}_2 = 4\hat{i}\text{ m}$ (East).
worked_examples.formula: Distance $d = s_1 + s_2$; Displacement $|\vec{s}| = \sqrt{s_1^2 + s_2^2}$; Direction $\theta = \arctan(s_1 / s_2)$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Distance is scalar sum: $3\text{ m} + 4\text{ m} = 7\text{ m}$.
2. Net vector $\vec{s} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$. Magnitude $= \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\text{ m}$.
3. Angle $\theta = \arctan(3/4) = 36.87^\circ$ North of East.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Distance = 7 m; (b) Displacement = 5 m at 36.9° North of East.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.4: Orthogonal vector addition triangle (3-4-5 right triangle)

worked_examples.problem: What does the odometer of an automobile measure? If the odometer reads 24830 km at the start of a journey and 25230 km at the end, what is the distance covered?
worked_examples.given: Odometer start $S_1 = 24830\text{ km}$, end $S_2 = 25230\text{ km}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. An odometer measures total actual distance (path length) traveled by the vehicle, regardless of twists, turns, or return trips.
2. Subtracting initial odometer reading from final gives the path length: $25230 - 24830 = 400\text{ km}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The odometer measures distance (path length); distance covered is 400 km.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.1: Automobile speedometer and digital odometer display

common_misconceptions.misconception: Displacement can be greater than distance if the object moves fast.
common_misconceptions.correction: Displacement is mathematically the straight line connecting two points, which is the shortest possible path in Euclidean geometry. Displacement can never exceed distance.
common_misconceptions.why_it_matters: Universal kinematic law tested on every Class 9 examination.

title: Rate of Motion: Speed, Velocity & The Geometry of Acceleration
description: Master uniform vs non-uniform motion, scalar speed vs vector velocity, average velocity formulations, and acceleration as the time rate of change of velocity.
subtopics: Uniform Motion: Equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line
Non-Uniform Motion: Unequal distances in equal intervals of time (accelerated/retarded)
Speed: Rate of distance coverage (v = d/t, SI unit m/s, km/h conversion * 5/18)
Velocity: Speed in a specified direction (v = s/t, vector)
Average Speed vs Average Velocity: Total distance / Total time vs (u + v) / 2 for uniform acceleration
Acceleration: Time rate of change of velocity (a = (v - u) / t, SI unit m/s^2)
key_concepts: Uniform Motion: Constant speed in a fixed straight-line direction with zero acceleration.
Speed vs Velocity: Speed is scalar magnitude; velocity includes directional orientation. Velocity changes if speed changes, direction changes, or both change.
Unit Conversion Constant: To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18; to convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5.
Average Velocity Equation: For uniformly changing velocity, v_avg = (u + v) / 2; generally v_avg = total displacement / total time.
Acceleration Formulation: a = (v - u) / t; positive when velocity increases (acceleration), negative when velocity decreases (retardation/deceleration).
Non-Zero Acceleration at Constant Speed: In circular motion, speed is constant but direction changes continuously, creating acceleration.
success_criteria: Student can convert units between km/h and m/s, calculate average speed vs average velocity, and compute acceleration/retardation with proper SI units.
chapter_notes:
### 4.4 Uniform vs Non-Uniform Motion
1. **Uniform Motion**: An object covers **equal distances in equal intervals of time**, no matter how small these time intervals are. Velocity is constant; acceleration $a = 0$.
2. **Non-Uniform Motion**: An object covers **unequal distances in equal intervals of time** (e.g., a car accelerating in city traffic).

### 4.5 Speed, Velocity & Acceleration
- **Speed ($v$)**: Distance / Time. Scalar, SI unit: $\text{m/s}$ or $\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$.
- **Velocity ($\vec{v}$)**: Displacement / Time. Vector, SI unit: $\text{m/s}$.
  $$\text{Average Speed} = \frac{\text{Total Distance Traversed}}{\text{Total Time Taken}}$$
  $$\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\text{Net Displacement}}{\text{Total Time Taken}} = \frac{u + v}{2} \quad \text{(for uniform acceleration)}$$
- **Unit Conversion Rule**:
  $$1 \text{ km/h} = \frac{1000\text{ m}}{3600\text{ s}} = \frac{5}{18}\text{ m/s}$$

### 4.6 Acceleration ($a$)
The measure of the rate of change of velocity of an object per unit time:
$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$
- Where $u = \text{initial velocity}$, $v = \text{final velocity}$, $t = \text{time interval}$.
- SI unit: **$\text{m/s}^2$** or **$\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$**.
- **Positive Acceleration**: $v > u$ (velocity increases in direction of motion).
- **Negative Acceleration (Retardation / Deceleration)**: $v < u$ (velocity decreases; $a < 0$).

worked_examples.problem: An object travels 16 m in 4 s and then another 16 m in 2 s. What is the average speed of the object?
worked_examples.given: Distance $d_1 = 16\text{ m}$, time $t_1 = 4\text{ s}$; Distance $d_2 = 16\text{ m}$, time $t_2 = 2\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.formula: Average Speed $v_{avg} = \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{d_1 + d_2}{t_1 + t_2}$.
worked_examples.calculation: $v_{avg} = \frac{32}{6} = \mathbf{5.33\text{ m/s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Average speed = 5.33 m/s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.5: Non-uniform motion interval timeline

worked_examples.problem: The odometer of a car reads 2000 km at the start of a trip and 2400 km at the end of the trip. If the trip took 8 h, calculate the average speed of the car in km/h and in m/s.
worked_examples.given: Distance $d = 2400 - 2000 = 400\text{ km}$. Time $t = 8\text{ h}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Speed in km/h: $v_{avg} = \frac{400}{8} = \mathbf{50\text{ km/h}}$.
2. Speed in m/s: $50 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{250}{18} = \mathbf{13.89\text{ m/s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Average speed = 50 km/h = 13.89 m/s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.6: Odometer trip distance and average speed calculation

worked_examples.problem: Usha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back along the same straight path. Find the average speed and average velocity of Usha.
worked_examples.given: Pool length $= 90\text{ m}$. Total distance $d = 90 + 90 = 180\text{ m}$. Total time $t = 1\text{ min} = 60\text{ s}$. Final position = Initial position.
worked_examples.formula: Average Speed $= \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}$; Average Velocity $= \frac{\text{Net Displacement}}{\text{Total Time}}$.
worked_examples.substitution: Average Speed $= \frac{180\text{ m}}{60\text{ s}}$; Net Displacement $= 0\text{ m} \implies \text{Average Velocity} = \frac{0}{60\text{ s}}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Average Speed $= \frac{180}{60} = \mathbf{3\text{ m/s}}$.
2. Since Usha returns to her starting point, her net displacement is zero.
3. Average Velocity $= \frac{0\text{ m}}{60\text{ s}} = \mathbf{0\text{ m/s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Average speed = 3 m/s; Average velocity = 0 m/s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.7: Swimming pool return path showing zero net displacement

worked_examples.problem: Starting from a stationary position, Rahul pedals his bicycle to attain a velocity of 6 m/s in 30 s. Then he applies brakes such that the velocity comes down to 4 m/s in the next 5 s. Calculate the acceleration of the bicycle in both cases.
worked_examples.given: Case 1: $u_1 = 0\text{ m/s}, v_1 = 6\text{ m/s}, t_1 = 30\text{ s}$. Case 2: $u_2 = 6\text{ m/s}, v_2 = 4\text{ m/s}, t_2 = 5\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Case 1 (speeding up): $a_1 = \frac{6}{30} = +\mathbf{0.2\text{ m/s}^2}$.
2. Case 2 (braking/retardation): $a_2 = \frac{-2}{5} = -\mathbf{0.4\text{ m/s}^2}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Acceleration in first case = +0.2 m/s²; in second case = -0.4 m/s² (retardation of 0.4 m/s²).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.8: Two-phase motion graph showing acceleration and deceleration

worked_examples.problem: A bus decreases its speed from 80 km/h to 60 km/h in 5 s. Find the acceleration of the bus.
worked_examples.given: Initial velocity $u = 80\text{ km/h} = 80 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{400}{18} = 22.22\text{ m/s}$. Final velocity $v = 60\text{ km/h} = 60 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{300}{18} = 16.67\text{ m/s}$. Time $t = 5\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation: $a = -\mathbf{1.11\text{ m/s}^2}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Acceleration = -1.11 m/s² (or retardation of 1.11 m/s²).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.9: Negative acceleration (deceleration) velocity profile

worked_examples.problem: A train starting from a railway station and moving with uniform acceleration attains a speed of 40 km/h in 10 minutes. Find its acceleration.
worked_examples.given: Initial velocity $u = 0\text{ m/s}$. Final velocity $v = 40\text{ km/h} = 40 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{100}{9}\text{ m/s} \approx 11.11\text{ m/s}$. Time $t = 10\text{ min} = 600\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation: $a = \frac{1}{54} \approx \mathbf{0.0185\text{ m/s}^2}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Acceleration = 0.0185 m/s² (or 1/54 m/s²).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.10: Uniform acceleration of train from rest

common_misconceptions.misconception: An object with constant speed can never have acceleration.
common_misconceptions.correction: In uniform circular motion, speed is strictly constant, but because the direction of motion continuously changes at every instant, velocity changes and the object experiences continuous inward centripetal acceleration.
common_misconceptions.why_it_matters: A classic CBSE board exam conceptual trap.

title: The Visual Language of Kinematics: Position-Time (s-t) & Velocity-Time (v-t) Master Graphs
description: Master graphical representation of motion: interpreting slope of distance-time graphs as speed, slope of velocity-time graphs as acceleration, and the area under velocity-time graphs as displacement.
subtopics: Distance-Time Graphs: Horizontal axis (time), Vertical axis (distance)
Interpreting s-t Slopes: Horizontal flat line = stationary; Straight inclined line = uniform speed; Curved line = accelerating
Mathematical Proof: Slope of s-t graph equals speed (Slope = Delta s / Delta t = v)
Velocity-Time Graphs: Horizontal flat line = constant velocity; Constant upward slope = uniform acceleration; Downward slope = uniform retardation
Mathematical Proof: Slope of v-t graph equals acceleration (Slope = Delta v / Delta t = a)
Area Under v-t Graph: Area under velocity-time curve represents magnitude of displacement (s = v * t)
key_concepts: Distance-Time Graph Slope: The gradient (slope = (s2 - s1) / (t2 - t1)) represents the speed of the moving object.
Stationary Object s-t Profile: A horizontal line parallel to the time axis indicates zero speed (object at rest).
Velocity-Time Graph Slope: The gradient (slope = (v2 - v1) / (t2 - t1)) represents the acceleration of the object.
Area Theorem of v-t Graphs: The geometric area bounded by the v-t curve and the time axis equals the exact displacement covered.
Rectangle + Triangle Decomposition: The area under a uniformly accelerating v-t curve decomposes into a lower rectangle (u * t) and an upper triangle (1/2 * a * t^2).

success_criteria: Student can extract speed from s-t slopes, extract acceleration from v-t slopes, and calculate displacement by computing area under v-t curves.
chapter_notes:
### 4.7 Graphical Analysis of Motion
Graphs provide a powerful visual method to describe basic properties of motion.

### 4.8 Distance-Time ($s-t$) Graphs
- **Horizontal line parallel to time axis**: Object is **at rest** (distance does not change as time advances; slope $= 0$).
- **Straight line passing through origin with constant slope**: **Uniform speed**.
  $$\text{Speed } v = \text{Slope} = \frac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$$
- **Steeper Slope**: Higher speed.
- **Curved line (parabola curving upward)**: **Non-uniform speed** (accelerating motion).

### 4.9 Velocity-Time ($v-t$) Graphs
- **Horizontal line parallel to time axis**: **Constant velocity** (zero acceleration; $a = 0$).
- **Straight line sloping upward**: **Uniform acceleration**.
  $$\text{Acceleration } a = \text{Slope} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$
- **Straight line sloping downward**: **Uniform retardation (deceleration)**.
- **THE AREA THEOREM**: The area enclosed by velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the **displacement** ($s$):
  $$\text{Displacement } s = \text{Area under } v-t \text{ curve}$$
  For uniform velocity: $\text{Area of Rectangle} = v \times t$.
  For uniform acceleration: $\text{Area of Trapezoid} = \text{Area of Rectangle } (u \times t) + \text{Area of Triangle } \left(\frac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)\right)$.

worked_examples.problem: Explain what physical quantity is represented by the slope of a distance-time graph. What does a horizontal line parallel to the time axis indicate?
worked_examples.given: Distance-time graph ($s-t$).
worked_examples.substitution: Change in distance divided by change in time.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Slope $= \frac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} = \text{Speed}$.
2. If the line is parallel to the time axis, $\Delta s = 0$ for any $\Delta t$.
3. Therefore, speed $= 0$, meaning the body is at rest (stationary).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The slope represents speed; a horizontal line parallel to the time axis indicates that the object is stationary (at rest).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.11: Distance-time graph showing uniform speed vs stationary state

worked_examples.problem: What physical quantity is determined by: (a) the slope of a velocity-time graph, and (b) the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph?
worked_examples.given: Velocity-time graph ($v-t$).
worked_examples.substitution: Slope has dimensions $[L T^{-1}] / [T] = [L T^{-2}]$; Area has dimensions $[L T^{-1}] \times [T] = [L]$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Slope of $v-t$ curve is the rate of change of velocity: $\frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \text{Acceleration} (a)$.
2. The area beneath the $v-t$ curve represents the product of velocity and time: $\text{Displacement} (s)$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Slope gives acceleration; (b) Area under the curve gives displacement (magnitude of distance).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.12: Velocity-time graph highlighting slope (acceleration) and area (displacement)

worked_examples.problem: A car accelerates uniformly from 18 km/h to 36 km/h in 5 s. Using a velocity-time graph, calculate: (a) the acceleration, and (b) the distance covered by the car.
worked_examples.given: $u = 18\text{ km/h} = 5\text{ m/s}, v = 36\text{ km/h} = 10\text{ m/s}, t = 5\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Acceleration: $a = \frac{5}{5} = \mathbf{1\text{ m/s}^2}$.
2. Distance: Area of rectangle under $u$ + Area of triangle under acceleration slope:
   $s = (u \times t) + \frac{1}{2}(v - u)t = (5 \times 5) + \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = 25 + 12.5 = \mathbf{37.5\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Acceleration = 1 m/s²; (b) Distance covered = 37.5 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.13: Trapezium area decomposition on v-t graph for uniform acceleration

worked_examples.problem: What can you say about the motion of an object whose distance-time graph is a curved parabolic line bending upwards?
worked_examples.given: Distance-time graph with increasing slope $\frac{ds}{dt}$.
worked_examples.substitution: Slope increases continuously as time progresses.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Tangent slope at any point gives instantaneous speed.
2. Since the slope becomes steeper with time, speed is continuously increasing.
3. This represents accelerated (non-uniform) motion.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The object is undergoing non-uniform accelerated motion where speed increases with time.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.14: Curved s-t graph indicating non-uniform accelerating motion

worked_examples.problem: A car traveling at constant speed of 20 m/s moves for 10 s. Draw its velocity-time graph and compute the distance covered from the graph.
worked_examples.given: Constant velocity $v = 20\text{ m/s}$, duration $t = 10\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation: $s = 20 \times 10 = \mathbf{200\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The v-t graph is a horizontal straight line at v = 20 m/s; distance covered = 200 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.15: Rectangular area under constant velocity-time graph

worked_examples.problem: Interpret a velocity-time graph that slopes linearly downwards from 25 m/s to 0 m/s in 5 s. Find the acceleration and stopping distance.
worked_examples.given: $u = 25\text{ m/s}, v = 0\text{ m/s}, t = 5\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Acceleration: $a = -\mathbf{5\text{ m/s}^2}$ (uniform retardation).
2. Distance: $s = \frac{125}{2} = \mathbf{62.5\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Acceleration = -5 m/s² (retardation = 5 m/s²); stopping distance = 62.5 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.16: Triangular area under uniform retardation velocity-time graph

title: Derivation & Architectural Calculus of the Three Kinematic Equations of Motion
description: Master the rigorous graphical derivation of the three fundamental equations of motion (v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2*at^2, v^2 - u^2 = 2as) from the geometry of the velocity-time trapezoid.
subtopics: First Equation of Motion: Velocity-Time relation derived from slope (v = u + at)
Second Equation of Motion: Position-Time relation derived from area decomposition (s = ut + 1/2*at^2)
Third Equation of Motion: Position-Velocity relation derived from trapezoid area formula (v^2 - u^2 = 2as)
Graphical Construction: Velocity-time trapezoid OABC with initial velocity u, final velocity v, and duration t
Algebraic Equivalence & Validation: Verifying units, dimensions, and limits for stationary start (u = 0)
NCERT Exemplar Calculations: Multi-parameter kinematic solutions
key_concepts: The Three Master Equations: The closed-form algebraic system governing 1D motion under constant acceleration.
Derivation of v = u + at: Gradient of line AB equals acceleration a = (v - u) / t, which rearranges to v = u + at.
Derivation of s = ut + 1/2*at^2: Area under AB equals sum of base rectangle OACD (u*t) and triangle ABD (1/2 * (v - u) * t = 1/2 * a * t^2).
Derivation of v^2 - u^2 = 2as: Area of trapezoid OABC = 1/2 * (sum of parallel sides) * height = 1/2 * (u + v) * t; substituting t = (v - u) / a gives 2as = v^2 - u^2.
Constant Acceleration Pre-Condition: These equations are valid ONLY when acceleration 'a' is strictly constant.
Rest and Braking Limits: If starting from rest, u = 0; if coming to a stop, v = 0 with negative acceleration.
success_criteria: Student can reproduce all three graphical derivations step-by-step with clean labeled diagrams and apply them to complex multi-step numerical problems.
chapter_notes:
### 4.10 The Three Equations of Motion
For an object moving with **uniform acceleration ($a$)**:
1. **Velocity-Time Relation**:
   $$v = u + at$$
2. **Position-Time Relation**:
   $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$
3. **Position-Velocity Relation**:
   $$v^2 - u^2 = 2as \iff v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

### 4.11 Step-by-Step Graphical Derivations
Consider the velocity-time graph of an object with initial velocity $u$ (at $t = 0$) accelerating uniformly to final velocity $v$ in time $t$.
- $OA = DC = u$ (initial velocity)
- $BC = v$ (final velocity)
- $OC = AD = t$ (time interval)
- $BD = BC - CD = v - u$ (change in velocity)

#### Derivation 1: $v = u + at$
$$\text{Slope } a = \frac{BD}{AD} = \frac{v - u}{t} \implies at = v - u \implies \mathbf{v = u + at}$$

#### Derivation 2: $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$
$$\text{Displacement } s = \text{Area of trapezoid } OABC = \text{Area of rectangle } OADC + \text{Area of } \triangle ABD$$
$$s = (OA \times OC) + \left(\frac{1}{2} \times AD \times BD\right)$$
$$s = (u \times t) + \left(\frac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)\right)$$
From equation 1, $v - u = at$. Substituting:
$$s = ut + \frac{1}{2} \times t \times (at) \implies \mathbf{s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2}$$

#### Derivation 3: $v^2 - u^2 = 2as$
$$\text{Area of trapezoid } OABC = \frac{\text{Sum of parallel sides} \times \text{Perpendicular distance}}{2} = \frac{(OA + BC) \times OC}{2} = \frac{(u + v)t}{2}$$
From equation 1, $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$. Substituting $t$:
$$s = \frac{(v + u)(v - u)}{2a} = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a} \implies 2as = v^2 - u^2 \implies \mathbf{v^2 - u^2 = 2as}$$

worked_examples.problem: A train starting from rest attains a velocity of 72 km/h in 5 minutes. Assuming that the acceleration is uniform, find: (a) the acceleration, and (b) the distance traveled by the train for attaining this velocity.
worked_examples.given: $u = 0\text{ m/s}$. $v = 72\text{ km/h} = 72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 20\text{ m/s}$. $t = 5\text{ min} = 300\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Acceleration: $a = \frac{1}{15} \approx \mathbf{0.067\text{ m/s}^2}$.
2. Distance: $s = \frac{1}{30} \times 90000 = \mathbf{3000\text{ m}} = \mathbf{3\text{ km}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Acceleration = 1/15 m/s² (0.067 m/s²); (b) Distance traveled = 3000 m (3 km).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.17: Kinematic derivation geometry for v = u + at

worked_examples.problem: Derive graphically the first equation of motion: v = u + at.
worked_examples.given: Velocity-time graph with initial velocity $u$ at $t=0$ and final velocity $v$ at time $t$.
worked_examples.substitution: $BC = BD - CD = v - u$; $AC = OD = t$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. From the graph, $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$.
2. Multiplying both sides by $t$: $at = v - u$.
3. Rearranging terms: $\mathbf{v = u + at}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: v = u + at (First equation of motion derived from slope of v-t graph).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.18: Standard NCERT graphical derivation figure for three kinematic equations

worked_examples.problem: Derive graphically the second equation of motion: s = ut + (1/2)at².
worked_examples.given: Displacement $s$ equals the total area of the trapezium $OABD$ beneath the $v-t$ graph.
worked_examples.formula: $\text{Area}(OABD) = \text{Area of rectangle } OADC + \text{Area of triangle } ACB$.
worked_examples.substitution: $\text{Area}(OADC) = OA \times OD = u \times t$; $\text{Area}(ACB) = \frac{1}{2} \times AC \times BC = \frac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. $s = u \cdot t + \frac{1}{2} t (v - u)$.
2. From the first equation, $v - u = at$.
3. Substitute $at$ for $(v - u)$: $s = ut + \frac{1}{2} t (at) = \mathbf{ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: s = ut + 1/2 at² (Second equation of motion derived from area decomposition).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.18: Area decomposition into rectangle and triangle beneath v-t line

worked_examples.problem: Derive graphically the third equation of motion: v² - u² = 2as.
worked_examples.given: Total distance $s$ is the area of trapezium $OABD$ with parallel sides $OA$ and $BD$.
worked_examples.formula: $s = \frac{\text{Sum of parallel sides} \times \text{Perpendicular distance}}{2} = \frac{(OA + BD) \times OD}{2}$.
worked_examples.substitution: $OA = u, BD = v, OD = t \implies s = \frac{(u + v)t}{2}$. From first equation, $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Substitute $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$ into the area formula:
   $s = \frac{(v + u)(v - u)}{2a}$.
2. Using algebraic identity $(v + u)(v - u) = v^2 - u^2$:
   $s = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$.
3. Multiplying both sides by $2a$: $\mathbf{2as = v^2 - u^2} \implies \mathbf{v^2 - u^2 = 2as}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: v² - u² = 2as (Third equation of motion relating velocity, acceleration, and displacement).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.18: Trapezium geometry for eliminating time t in kinematic derivation

worked_examples.problem: The brakes applied to a car produce an acceleration of 6 m/s² in the opposite direction to the motion. If the car takes 2 s to stop after the application of brakes, calculate the distance it travels during this time.
worked_examples.given: $a = -6\text{ m/s}^2$ (retardation). $t = 2\text{ s}$. Final velocity $v = 0\text{ m/s}$.
worked_examples.formula: $v = u + at \implies u = v - at$; $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Initial velocity: $u = 12\text{ m/s}$.
2. Distance: $s = 24 - \frac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 24 - 12 = \mathbf{12\text{ m}}$.

title: Braking Dynamics, Reaction Time & Multi-Phase Motion Engineering
description: Master real-world kinematic applications: stopping distance calculations, driver reaction times, negative acceleration (retardation), and vertical free fall under gravity (g = 9.8 m/s^2).
subtopics: Retardation Mechanics: Velocity vector opposed by negative acceleration vector
Stopping Distance Formula: s_stop = u^2 / (2*a) and quadratic velocity dependence
Driver Reaction Time: Constant speed distance traveled during neural perception lag (d_react = u * t_r)
Total Stopping Distance: d_total = d_reaction + d_braking
Free Fall Kinematics: Acceleration due to gravity g = 9.8 m/s^2 (a = -g for upward ascent)
Symmetry of Vertical Motion: Time of ascent = Time of descent; Impact velocity = Launch velocity
key_concepts: Retardation / Deceleration: Acceleration vector pointing in opposite direction to velocity, causing speed to drop.
Quadratic Stopping Distance: Doubling vehicle speed quadruples the required braking distance (s proportional to u^2).
Two-Phase Braking Model: Total distance = Perception phase (constant speed u*t_r) + Braking phase (u^2 / 2a).
Free Fall Under Gravity: All objects in vacuum accelerate downward at constant g = 9.8 m/s^2 regardless of mass.
Vertical Ascent Sign Convention: Taking upward as positive: a = -g = -9.8 m/s^2; at maximum peak, v = 0.

success_criteria: Student can calculate vehicle stopping distances under varied speeds, evaluate reaction time lag, and solve vertical projectile problems using g = 9.8 m/s^2.
chapter_notes:
### 4.12 Retardation & Braking Dynamics
When brakes are applied, the acceleration acts in the opposite direction to velocity ($a < 0$).
From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, setting final velocity $v = 0$ (car stops):
$$0 = u^2 - 2as \implies s_{\text{braking}} = \frac{u^2}{2a}$$
**CRITICAL INSIGHT**: Stopping distance is proportional to the **square of velocity** ($s \propto u^2$).
- If speed doubles ($2\times$), stopping distance increases **$4\times$**!
- If speed triples ($3\times$), stopping distance increases **$9\times$**!

### 4.13 Reaction Time and Total Stopping Distance
$$\text{Total Stopping Distance} = s_{\text{reaction}} + s_{\text{braking}} = (u \times t_r) + \frac{u^2}{2a}$$
Where $t_r$ is the human driver's neural perception-reaction time (~$0.2 - 0.7\text{ s}$).

### 4.14 Vertical Motion Under Gravity
When an object is thrown vertically upwards:
- Acceleration $a = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ (downward acceleration opposes upward motion).
- At the **highest point**, final velocity **$v = 0$**.
- Maximum height reached: $h_{\text{max}} = \frac{u^2}{2g}$.
- Time of ascent: $t_{\text{up}} = \frac{u}{g}$.
- Total flight time: $T = 2 \times t_{\text{up}} = \frac{2u}{g}$.

worked_examples.problem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of 5 m/s. If the acceleration of the ball during its motion is 10 m/s² in the downward direction, what will be the height attained by the ball and how much time will it take to reach there?

worked_examples.formula: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \implies s = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$; $v = u + at \implies t = \frac{v - u}{a}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Maximum height: $s = \frac{25}{20} = \mathbf{1.25\text{ m}}$.
2. Time taken to reach top: $t = \frac{5}{10} = \mathbf{0.5\text{ s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Height attained = 1.25 m; Time taken to reach maximum height = 0.5 s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.21: Vertical projectile trajectory under gravitational acceleration

worked_examples.problem: A car driver traveling at 25 m/s sees an obstruction and hits the brakes after a reaction time of 0.2 s. The brakes produce a deceleration of 5 m/s². Calculate the total stopping distance of the car.
worked_examples.given: Speed $u = 25\text{ m/s}$, reaction time $t_r = 0.2\text{ s}$, deceleration $a = -5\text{ m/s}^2$.

worked_examples.calculation:

worked_examples.problem: Explain why time of ascent equals time of descent for an object thrown vertically upward in the absence of air resistance.
worked_examples.given: Symmetric gravitational flight: ascent from ground to $h_{max}$ and descent from $h_{max}$ to ground.
worked_examples.calculation:

title: Motion in a Plane: Uniform Circular Motion (UCM) & Radial Acceleration
description: Master uniform circular motion: why motion with constant speed along a circular trajectory is perpetually accelerated, tangential velocity vectors, and centripetal kinematics.
subtopics: Circular Trajectory Mechanics: Path with continuously changing direction
Uniform Circular Motion Definition: Circular motion at constant scalar speed
Why UCM is Accelerated: Continuously rotating velocity vector requires net centripetal acceleration
Orbital Speed Formula: v = 2*pi*r / T
Tangential Velocity Demonstration: Whirling stone on string released flies off along tangent
Real-World UCM Systems: Artificial earth satellites, tip of clock hands, moon around earth
key_concepts: UCM Definition: When an object moves in a circular path with constant speed, its motion is called Uniform Circular Motion.
Perpetual Acceleration Invariant: Even though speed is invariant, the continuous turning of the velocity direction vector makes UCM an accelerated motion.
Tangential Direction: The instantaneous velocity vector at any point on the circle points along the tangent to the circle at that point.
UCM Speed Formula: v = (2 * pi * r) / T, where r is orbital radius and T is period of revolution.
Centripetal Inward Force: An inward acceleration (a = v^2 / r) directed toward the circle center is required to maintain the curved path.
Inertial Tangential Release: When the centripetal constraint is severed (e.g. string breaks), the object continues straight along the instantaneous tangent.
success_criteria: Student can explain why circular motion with constant speed is accelerated, compute orbital speeds via v = 2*pi*r / T, and predict tangential release trajectories.
chapter_notes:
### 4.15 Uniform Circular Motion (UCM)
When an object moves in a **circular path with uniform (constant) speed**, its motion is termed **Uniform Circular Motion**.

### 4.16 Why is UCM an Accelerated Motion?
- Velocity is a **vector** having both magnitude (speed) and direction.
- In circular motion, although speed remains constant, the **direction of motion changes continuously at every point**.
- Because velocity changes direction continuously, there is a continuous change in velocity with time.
- Therefore, **Uniform Circular Motion is an accelerated motion**!
- The acceleration is directed radially inward toward the center and is called **Centripetal Acceleration**:
  $$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

### 4.17 Calculating Speed in UCM
For a circular path of radius $r$, the circumference is $2\pi r$. If an object takes $T$ seconds to complete one revolution:
$$v = \frac{\text{Circumference}}{\text{Time Period}} = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

### 4.18 Tangential Release (Activity 4.11)
- Whirling a stone tied to a thread in a circular path: The stone moves in a circle because the thread exerts an inward centripetal tension.
- If the thread breaks or is released, the stone **flies off in a straight line along the tangent** to the circular path at that instant!
- This proves that at every instant, the velocity vector is directed along the **tangent** to the circle.

worked_examples.calculation: $v = \frac{265464.58}{86400} \approx \mathbf{3.07\text{ km/s}} = \mathbf{3072.5\text{ m/s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Orbital speed = 3.07 km/s (3073 m/s).

3. A change in the direction of velocity constitutes an acceleration ($a_c = v^2/r$ directed towards the center).
4. Therefore, uniform circular motion is inherently accelerated motion.

worked_examples.calculation:
1. While whirled, tension in the string pulls the stone inward, continuously bending its path into a circle.
2. At the exact instant the string breaks or is released, centripetal force drops to zero.
3. By inertia of motion, the stone continues in a straight line along the direction of its instantaneous velocity, which is tangential to the circular path at that release point.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The stone flies off tangentially to the circular path due to directional inertia.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.30: Tangential straight-line trajectory upon release of whirled stone

worked_examples.problem: A cyclist moves around a circular track of radius 70 m in 44 s at uniform speed. Calculate the cyclist's speed and magnitude of displacement after 22 s.
worked_examples.given: Radius $r = 70\text{ m}$, Period $T = 44\text{ s}$, Time $t = 22\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.formula: $v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$; Displacement after half lap ($t = T/2$) $= 2r$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Speed $v = \frac{440}{44} = \mathbf{10\text{ m/s}}$.
2. In 22 s ($T/2$), the cyclist reaches the diametrically opposite point.
3. Displacement $= 2 \times 70 = \mathbf{140\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Speed = 10 m/s; Magnitude of displacement = 140 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.31: Half-lap displacement on circular track

worked_examples.problem: Contrast linear velocity and centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion in terms of direction.
worked_examples.given: Particle in UCM with position vector $\vec{r}$, velocity $\vec{v}$, and acceleration $\vec{a}_c$.
worked_examples.substitution: $\vec{v}$ is along the tangent; $\vec{a}_c$ is directed radially inwards along the radius toward the center.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Tangential velocity $\vec{v}$ is tangent to the circle: $\vec{v} = v\hat{\theta}$.
2. Centripetal acceleration $\vec{a}_c$ points along the radius inward: $\vec{a}_c = -\frac{v^2}{r}\hat{r}$.
3. The angle between them is identically $90^\circ$ (orthogonal) at every instant.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Linear velocity is directed tangentially, while centripetal acceleration is directed radially inward towards the centre; they are mutually perpendicular.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.32: Perpendicular relationship between velocity and centripetal acceleration

chapter_notes:
### 4.19 Comprehensive NCERT Exercise Solutions Ledger

#### Q1. Athlete on Circular Track
- $D = 200\text{ m} \implies r = 100\text{ m}$. Time for 1 round $= 40\text{ s}$.
- Time $t = 2\text{ min } 20\text{ s} = 140\text{ s}$.
- Number of rounds $= 140/40 = 3.5$.
- **Distance** $= 3.5 \times 2\pi r = 3.5 \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 100 = \mathbf{2200\text{ m}}$.
- **Displacement** $=$ Straight line between diametrically opposite points $= 2r = \mathbf{200\text{ m}}$.

#### Q2. Joseph's Jogging Trajectory
- Point $A$ to $B$: $300\text{ m}$ in $2\text{ min } 50\text{ s} = 170\text{ s}$.
  * Average Speed $= 300 / 170 = \mathbf{1.76\text{ m/s}}$.
  * Average Velocity $= 300 / 170 = \mathbf{1.76\text{ m/s}}$ (along $AB$).
- Point $A$ to $C$ (turns back $100\text{ m}$ in $1\text{ min} = 60\text{ s}$):
  * Total Distance $= 300 + 100 = 400\text{ m}$. Total Time $= 170 + 60 = 230\text{ s}$.
  * **Average Speed** $= 400 / 230 = \mathbf{1.74\text{ m/s}}$.
  * Net Displacement $= 300 - 100 = 200\text{ m}$.
  * **Average Velocity** $= 200 / 230 = \mathbf{0.87\text{ m/s}}$ (along $AB$).

#### Q3. Abdul's Commute Average Speed
- Let distance to school be $x\text{ km}$.
- Time to go: $t_1 = x / 20$. Time to return: $t_2 = x / 30$.
- Total distance $= 2x$. Total time $= x/20 + x/30 = 5x / 60 = x / 12$.
- **Average Speed** $= \frac{2x}{x/12} = 2 \times 12 = \mathbf{24\text{ km/h}}$.
*(Notice: NOT the simple arithmetic average of 25 km/h, but the harmonic mean: $\frac{2 \times 20 \times 30}{20 + 30} = 24\text{ km/h}$!)*

#### Q4. Motorboat Acceleration
- Starts from rest: $u = 0$. Acceleration $a = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Time $t = 8.0\text{ s}$.
- $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 3.0 \times (8)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 64 = \mathbf{96\text{ m}}$.

#### Q5. Two Braking Cars v-t Comparison
- Car 1: $u_1 = 52\text{ km/h} = 52 \times \frac{5}{18} = 14.44\text{ m/s}$. Stops in $t_1 = 5\text{ s}$.
  * Distance covered $s_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 14.44 = \mathbf{36.1\text{ m}}$.
- Car 2: $u_2 = 3\text{ km/h} = 3 \times \frac{5}{18} = 0.833\text{ m/s}$. Stops in $t_2 = 10\text{ s}$.
  * Distance covered $s_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 0.833 = \mathbf{4.17\text{ m}}$.
- **Conclusion**: Car 1 traveled much farther ($36.1\text{ m}$ vs $4.17\text{ m}$) after the application of brakes.

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Ex Q1. An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 200 m in 40 s. What will be the distance covered and the displacement at the end of 2 minutes 20 s?
worked_examples.given: $D = 200\text{ m} \implies r = 100\text{ m}$. Time for 1 round $= 40\text{ s}$. Total time $t = 140\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.formula: Rounds $n = \frac{140}{40} = 3.5$. Distance $s = 3.5 \times 2\pi r$. Displacement across diameter $= 2r = D$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Distance $= 3.5 \times 628.57 = \mathbf{2200\text{ m}}$.
2. Displacement $= \mathbf{200\text{ m}}$ (straight-line diameter).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Distance = 2200 m; Displacement = 200 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.3: Athlete circular track trajectory

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Ex Q2. Joseph jogs from one end A to the other end B of a straight 300 m road in 2 min 50 s and then turns around and jogs 100 m back to point C in another 1 min. What are Joseph's average speeds and velocities in jogging: (a) from A to B, and (b) from A to C?
worked_examples.given: Path $AB = 300\text{ m}, t_1 = 170\text{ s}$. Path $BC = 100\text{ m}, t_2 = 60\text{ s}$. Total time to C $= 230\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.substitution: (a) $A \to B$: Dist = 300 m, Disp = 300 m, Time = 170 s. (b) $A \to C$: Dist = 400 m, Disp = 200 m, Time = 230 s.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. From A to B:
   - Average Speed $= 300 / 170 = \mathbf{1.76\text{ m/s}}$.
   - Average Velocity $= 300 / 170 = \mathbf{1.76\text{ m/s}}$ (along AB).
2. From A to C:
   - Average Speed $= 400 / 230 = \mathbf{1.74\text{ m/s}}$.
   - Average Velocity $= (300 - 100) / 230 = 200 / 230 = \mathbf{0.87\text{ m/s}}$ (along AC).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) From A to B: Avg Speed = 1.76 m/s, Avg Velocity = 1.76 m/s. (b) From A to C: Avg Speed = 1.74 m/s, Avg Velocity = 0.87 m/s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.33: Joseph's straight jogging trajectory and reverse turn displacement

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Ex Q3. Abdul, while driving to school, computes the average speed for his trip to be 20 km/h. On his return trip along the same route, there is less traffic and the average speed is 30 km/h. What is the average speed for Abdul's trip?
worked_examples.given: Let one-way distance be $x\text{ km}$. Speed to school $v_1 = 20\text{ km/h}$. Speed returning $v_2 = 30\text{ km/h}$.
worked_examples.formula: Average Speed $= \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{2x}{t_1 + t_2} = \frac{2x}{\frac{x}{v_1} + \frac{x}{v_2}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$ (Harmonic Mean).
worked_examples.calculation: $v_{avg} = \frac{1200}{50} = \mathbf{24\text{ km/h}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Average speed for Abdul's round trip = 24 km/h (Note: it is NOT the arithmetic average 25 km/h).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.6: Round trip harmonic mean average speed diagram

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Ex Q4. A motorboat starting from rest on a lake accelerates in a straight line at a constant rate of 3.0 m/s² for 8.0 s. How far does the boat travel during this time?
worked_examples.given: $u = 0\text{ m/s}, a = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2, t = 8.0\text{ s}$.
worked_examples.calculation: $s = 1.5 \times 64 = \mathbf{96\text{ m}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The motorboat travels 96 m.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.20: Straight-line boat acceleration profile

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Ex Q7. A ball is gently dropped from a height of 20 m. If its velocity increases uniformly at the rate of 10 m/s², with what velocity will it strike the ground? After what time will it strike the ground?
worked_examples.given: $u = 0\text{ m/s}, s = 20\text{ m}, a = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Impact speed: $v = \mathbf{20\text{ m/s}}$.
2. Time of fall: $t = \frac{20}{10} = \mathbf{2\text{ s}}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Impact velocity = 20 m/s; Time taken = 2 s.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Fig. 4.22: Free fall from 20 m height under gravity

common_misconceptions.correction: Average speed is (v1 + v2) / 2 ONLY if the object travels at those speeds for EQUAL INTERVALS OF TIME. When traveling EQUAL DISTANCES, you must compute total distance divided by total time, which yields the harmonic mean: 2*v1*v2 / (v1 + v2).
common_misconceptions.why_it_matters: The single most tested numerical trap on CBSE Class 9 mid-term and final exams.
